title: The Line the Thing Draws Itself: Beaune, the Bay of Naples, and the Track at the Edge of the Wood
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Wine Town and the Pulse

stops.name: Beaune, the wine agent's only son
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia, corroborated in the dossier crawl against the BnF authority record and an Académie de médecine eulogy
stops.campa: In the Côte-d'Or town where the hospices sell their wine at auction and the vineyards climb the slope behind the walls, Claude Charles Marey represents the wine trade. He and Thérèse-Joséphine Bernard have one child and will have no other. The streets the boy grows up in are cellars and coopers' yards, and the trade around him runs on waiting: sugar turns to alcohol at its own speed, and the year is the smallest unit anything gets counted in. The instruments he builds later will divide a second into twelve parts, and then into hundreds. He is born on the fifth of March 1830.
suggested_refs: The wine town of Beaune, Côte-d'Or, and the Hospices auction

stops.name: Collège Monge, Beaune: the baccalaureate and three futures
stops.date_confidence: the literary baccalaureate is dated 1849 by the Beaune municipal archive account; no month is given and August is a default for ordering. The anecdote of three competing family wishes is repeated in institutional biographies with no contemporary letter behind it and is [R]. The building coordinate is approximate, in the Beaune old town.
stops.campa: He does his secondary studies at the town college named for Monge, the geometer of Beaune, and comes out in 1849 with a literary baccalaureate. Three futures are pulled at him at once. His mother wants a priest. His father wants a physician. The boy himself draws machines and wants to build them. Medicine is settled on, the compromise nobody chose. He keeps the drawing and the machines. No letter from any of the three survives to say how the argument went, or whether there was one.
suggested_refs: Collège Monge, Beaune, named for Gaspard Monge

stops.name: Faculté de médecine, Paris: the compromise begun
stops.date_confidence: 1849 attested for the start of medical study in Paris (fr.wikipedia chronology, 1849-1859); no month, November defaulted for the academic year. Coordinate corrected: the historic faculty at 12 rue de l'École-de-Médecine is at 48.8516, 2.3411, about 190 m from the value the geography lens carried.
stops.campa: He comes up to Paris and enters the faculty in the rue de l'École-de-Médecine with ten years of study ahead of him. The anatomy theatres teach him bodies opened after they have stopped. What holds him is the opposite case: the body while it is still running, the pulse under a fingertip, the heart striking the ribs from the inside. Neither the scalpel nor the ear laid on a chest can hold such a thing still long enough to set it beside another one and compare. He starts looking early for something that can.
sources: fr.wikipedia, Musée d'histoire de la médecine de Paris
suggested_refs: The Faculté de médecine de Paris, 12 rue de l'École-de-Médecine

stops.name: Hôpital Cochin, first in the competition
stops.date_confidence: the internship is dated 1854-1858 by the institutional biography relayed in the dossier crawl; no month attested, January defaulted. The placing-first detail reaches me only through that summary and is [R]; Beau and Cochin are [A]. Coordinate corrected to fr.wikipedia's value for Cochin at 27 rue du Faubourg-Saint-Jacques, about 380 m from the geography lens's figure.
stops.campa: He takes first place in the competitive examination for the Paris hospital internship and goes into the service of Joseph-Simon Beau at Cochin, where he stays four years. Beau holds a view of the heartbeat that Marey will spend the next decade dismantling. The wards run on argument: whether the shock felt at the chest wall belongs to the contraction of the ventricle or to something else entirely, and nobody can settle it, because the whole dispute is being conducted between two men's fingertips and two men's ears.
suggested_refs: Hôpital Cochin, 27 rue du Faubourg-Saint-Jacques, Paris

stops.name: Faculté de médecine, the thesis on the circulation of the blood
stops.date_confidence: attested; academie-medecine.fr, and the published thesis (Paris: Rignoux, 1859) cited in the dossier bibliography
stops.campa: One day short of his twenty-ninth birthday he defends Recherches sur la circulation du sang à l'état physiologique et dans les maladies, before a jury presided over by Jules Gavarret, the physicist turned physician who had spent his career trying to put numbers into French medicine. Gavarret will preside once more, five years on, over the academy dispute that goes Marey's way. Rignoux prints the thesis the same year. He is now a doctor of medicine and will never, on any evidence reachable, treat a patient.
suggested_refs: Recherches sur la circulation du sang à l'état physiologique et dans les maladies (Paris: Rignoux, 1859)

segments.name: The Instrument That Writes By Itself

stops.name: École vétérinaire d'Alfort, Donders makes an introduction
stops.date_confidence: 1859 and the Donders introduction are stated outright by academie-medecine.fr, which upgrades this from the [R] the geography lens assigned to [A]; no month is given and June is a default. Coordinate corrected to the school campus at 7 avenue du Général-de-Gaulle, about 580 m from the lens's value, which fell off the grounds.
stops.campa: The Dutch physiologist Frans Cornelius Donders puts him in the way of Auguste Chauveau, who runs physiology at the veterinary school across the Marne. Chauveau has what Marey lacks, which is horses and the standing to open them. Marey has what Chauveau lacks, which is an instinct for levers, watch springs, and stretched rubber. Neither of them has the instrument the question needs, because nobody has made it. The work in this yard runs four years and ends an argument no stethoscope had been able to end.
suggested_refs: The École vétérinaire d'Alfort, Maisons-Alfort

stops.name: Rue Cuvier, the laboratory paid for out of pocket
stops.date_confidence: dated c.1859-1863 by the Beaune municipal archive account; October 1859 is a default for ordering, not an attested month. The exact house number in the rue Cuvier is not located and the pin is street-level. The claim that this was the first private laboratory of experimental physiology in Paris is a later institutional boast with no census behind it and is [R].
stops.campa: In his own rooms in the rue Cuvier, a few steps from the Jardin des Plantes, he sets up a laboratory at his own expense, because no institution will give him one. Later histories call it the first private laboratory of experimental physiology in Paris. It is a workshop before it is a laboratory: a lathe, watch springs, drums of stretched membrane, cylinders of paper blackened over a lamp. The instruments he needs do not exist and cannot be bought, so he makes them. Nothing reachable says what he lived on in these years, or whose money paid for the lathe.
stops.quote: Registering apparatus only can supply this need, for they faithfully render all the phases of motion communicated to them.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), on why the unaided eye cannot follow rapid motion
suggested_refs: The rue Cuvier, beside the Jardin des Plantes, Paris 5e

stops.name: Paris, the sphygmograph: the pulse writes itself down
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict and the conflict is not resolved here. fr.wikipedia has the device built in 1859 and presented to the Académie des sciences in 1860 with Chauveau; academie-medecine.fr says it was presented in 1860 to the Société de biologie; en.wikipedia dates the Chauveau and Breguet wearable version to 1859. Built 1859, presented 1860, presenting body disputed; January is a default. The pin is the Institut de France, correct only if the Académie des sciences account is.
stops.campa: Karl von Vierordt had already built a machine that drew the pulse, and it was a heavy apparatus that could not leave a table. Marey, with the Breguet watchmakers, builds one that straps to a wrist: a spring rides the artery, a stylus rides the spring, a strip of smoked paper carries away an unbroken line of every beat. The pulse stops being something a physician feels and becomes something anyone can read, hours later and in another city. He presents it in 1860. The sources disagree on whether he presented it to the Académie des sciences or to the Société de biologie.
suggested_refs: Surviving Marey sphygmographs, Musée Marey, Beaune
Karl von Vierordt's table sphygmograph, the instrument superseded

stops.name: Alfort, probes in the heart of a standing horse
stops.date_confidence: 1861 is the dossier crawl's date for the start of the intensive cardiographic work; the joint memoir Appareils et expériences cardiographiques is 1863. No month attested, January defaulted. [A]. The 1884 anti-vivisection pamphlet listed under sources names Marey among physiologists who cut into living animals; it is a real one-directional engagement with this work and is cited here rather than staged as a scene.
stops.campa: Chauveau passes pressure-transmitting probes down the great vessels of a standing horse, into the right atrium and the right ventricle, and Marey's drums write those pressures as curves on the same turning cylinder that carries the trace taken from the chest wall outside. Three lines, one clock. Read together they show that the shock a physician feels at the ribs falls with the contraction of the ventricle. The question had been argued for a generation on the evidence of what men believed they had heard. The horse stands quietly through it, and the cylinder turns.
sources: Chauveau and Marey, Appareils et expériences cardiographiques (1863), via the dossier crawl
The Vivisectors' Directory, ed. Benjamin Bryan, pref. Frances Power Cobbe (Victoria Street Society, London, 1884), which names Marey; verified at gutenberg.org/files/54233
suggested_refs: Appareils et expériences cardiographiques, Chauveau and Marey, 1863

stops.name: Académie de médecine, Gavarret closes the question
stops.date_confidence: the controversy and its closure in Marey and Chauveau's favour are reported from Académie de médecine proceedings through the dossier crawl and were not independently verified; July 1864 is given, with no day, and the tag is [R] on that basis. Coordinate corrected to fr.wikipedia's value for the Académie nationale de médecine in the rue Bonaparte, about 230 m from the geography lens's figure, which was repeated wrongly at four indices.
stops.campa: The dispute reaches the academy floor: Beau, under whom Marey served at Cochin, against the traces brought back from Alfort. Jules Gavarret, who had presided over Marey's thesis five years before, closes it in favour of the cardiographic reading. What decides it is not eloquence and not seniority. One side can lay a sheet of smoked paper on the table and put a finger on the place in the line where the ventricle tightens; the other side can only say again what it believes it felt. Marey is thirty-four, holds no chair, no hospital post and no salary, and has just won an argument against his own former chief.
suggested_refs: Bulletin de l'Académie de médecine, session of July 1864

stops.name: Rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, the laboratory in Molière's room
stops.date_confidence: the Beaune archive dates the move only to the 1860s; 1865 is a placement for ordering and not an attested year. The claim that the room was a former performance space associated with Molière's company is a later institutional recollection, not independently confirmed, and is [R]. The 1863 publication of Physiologie médicale de la circulation du sang, carried in this campa, is [A] from the dossier bibliography.
stops.campa: He moves the laboratory into the rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, to a room the house remembers as a stage of Molière's company. Whatever the truth of that, it now holds tambours, cylinders, and a growing menagerie of devices for making motion visible; visitors describe a clockmaker's shop invaded by a hospital. He is thirty-five and still has no salaried post of any kind. Two years earlier he had published Physiologie médicale de la circulation du sang, the gathered work of the cardiographic years.
sources: Physiologie médicale de la circulation du sang (Paris: Adrien Delahaye, 1863)
suggested_refs: The rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, Paris 6e

stops.name: Collège de France, deputy and then the chair
stops.date_confidence: deputy to Pierre Flourens from 1867 and succession to the chair of histoire naturelle des corps organisés in 1869 are both in fr.wikipedia's chronology; no month, November defaulted for the academic year. Contradiction flagged, not resolved: the Collège's own succession table reads 1869-1903, against the 1869-1904 carried by the chronologies and obituaries. Coordinate corrected to 11 place Marcelin-Berthelot, about 200 m from the lens's value. Du mouvement dans les fonctions de la vie (1868) is [R], from the dossier bibliography.
stops.campa: He becomes deputy to Pierre Flourens in 1867, and two years later takes the chair of the natural history of organised bodies, which he holds for the rest of his life. The lectures of 1868 go into print as Du mouvement dans les fonctions de la vie, and the title is the entire programme: not the organs, not the tissues, but movement itself as the thing physiology ought to be measuring. He has a public platform now and a laboratory allowance. He goes on building most of the instruments with his own hands.
stops.quote: The comparison of animals with machines is not only legitimate, it is also extremely useful from different points of view.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), Introduction, p.1
suggested_refs: The chair of histoire naturelle des corps organisés, Collège de France

stops.name: Rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie, the artificial insect
stops.date_confidence: 1869 and the apparatus are attested in en.wikipedia, which specifies gold foil and a soot-covered glass fibre; the dossier's gold foil and light is wrong and the correction is taken, since the trace was inscribed mechanically and not photographically. No month is attested and December is a default chosen to place the stop after the chair within the same year; the true order of the two is unknown. The siting at the rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie laboratory is inference from the period, not an attested venue.
stops.campa: A live insect's wing beats too fast to see and far too fast to photograph. So he builds a false one. Gold foil for the wing, driven mechanically, its tip carrying a fine fibre against a glass plate blackened with soot. The wing scratches its own path into the lampblack, and the path is a figure of eight. Nothing here is photographed and nothing here is alive; the record is a scratch in soot, made by the moving thing itself. He is thirty-nine, and has spent ten years building instruments.
stops.quote: Would it be impossible for us to reproduce a phenomenon which we understand? We will not carry our scepticism so far.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), Introduction
suggested_refs: Marey's artificial insect, Musée Marey, Beaune

stops.name: Paris, La Machine animale and the horse in the air
stops.date_confidence: publication attested for 1873 (Germer-Baillière) in both the English and French chronologies; no month, January defaulted. The election to the Académie nationale de médecine in 1872 is from the dossier's institutional table. Placed at his laboratory address, where the work was done, rather than at a publisher's premises. Muybridge's 1878 Palo Alto sequence is cited here as the later answer to this book's claim; Marey's body was never in California and no Palo Alto stop exists in this file.
stops.campa: Elected to the Académie de médecine the year before, he publishes La Machine animale: locomotion terrestre et aérienne. In it he states, on mechanical traces alone and before any photograph could show it, that the galloping horse leaves the ground with its legs gathered under the body and not stretched fore and aft as two centuries of painters had drawn them. An English translation follows in 1874 as Animal Mechanism and carries the claim across the Atlantic, to a country where a railroad millionaire is already paying a photographer to settle a related bet.
stops.quote: Living beings have been frequently and in every age compared to machines, but it is only in the present day that the bearing and the justice of this comparison are fully comprehensible.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism: A Treatise on Terrestrial and Aerial Locomotion (D. Appleton and Company, New York), Introduction, opening lines
sources: muybridge.journey.json, on Leland Stanford's commission and the 1878 Horse in Motion
suggested_refs: La Machine animale (Paris: Germer-Baillière, 1873)
Animal Mechanism, International Scientific Series vol. XI, London and New York, 1874

stops.name: Institut de France, Claude Bernard's seat and the graphic method
stops.date_confidence: both the election to the Académie des sciences in Claude Bernard's seat and the publication of La Méthode graphique dans les sciences expérimentales (G. Masson) are attested to 1878; no months are given and January is a default for ordering. Bernard died in February 1878.
stops.campa: This year he publishes La Méthode graphique dans les sciences expérimentales, which is less a book about physiology than a manifesto for a way of knowing anything at all: put a stylus on every process that moves, let the process inscribe itself, and read the curve instead of the witness. Testimony is unreliable, he argues, and the senses that produce it are worse. Claude Bernard has died in February, and in the same year Marey is elected to his seat at the Académie des sciences, beneath the dome.
stops.quote: While observation employed alone furnishes only incomplete and sometimes false data, the graphic method carries its precision into the analysis of the very complex movements concerned in locomotion.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), on the paces of quadrupeds and the authors from Borelli onward
suggested_refs: La Méthode graphique dans les sciences expérimentales (Paris: G. Masson, 1878)

segments.name: The Bay of Naples and the Bird in the Air

stops.name: Stazione Zoologica, Naples: a request for live torpedo rays
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia records the request to Anton Dohrn's station for live torpedo rays on 1 November 1876, which puts the Naples connection four years before the villa and corrects the dossier's dating of it to the 1880s. Coordinate corrected to en.wikipedia's value for the Stazione Zoologica, about 530 m from the geography lens's figure. Whether Marey came in person for this request is not stated in the source.
stops.campa: Anton Dohrn's zoological station on the shore below the Villa Comunale keeps the Mediterranean alive in tanks for any laboratory in Europe that writes and asks. On the first of November Marey writes and asks: torpedo rays, living ones, the fish that carries its own electricity in its flanks. The station is a supply house and a laboratory at once, and he will use it for the rest of his life. This is the first of the letters between him and the station, and it is dated 1876.
suggested_refs: The Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn, Naples

stops.name: Paris, the letter to Gaston Tissandier
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated 1878 in the dossier's narrative of the Marey-Muybridge exchange and in the hekint.org essay; I never saw the text or a printed transcription, so it is [R] and the wording below is paraphrase. No month, December defaulted after La Nature's reproduction of the Palo Alto plates. The office of La Nature is not pinned and the corpus's general Paris coordinate stands in, the specific-pin discipline having nothing specific to work with here.
stops.campa: La Nature reproduces the plates in which Eadweard Muybridge, working for Leland Stanford at Palo Alto, has caught a galloping horse with all four feet off the ground and the legs gathered exactly as La Machine animale had said they would be. Marey writes to the editor, Gaston Tissandier. The pictures are admirable; would he please put him in contact with the man who made them. Then, in the same letter, he describes the thing he wants next, which does not exist. A gun, photographic, fired at a bird in flight.
sources: hekint.org, Étienne-Jules Marey (1830-1904): the study of movement in the functions of life
muybridge.journey.json, on the 1878 Horse in Motion
suggested_refs: La Nature, ed. Gaston Tissandier, issues of 1878 reproducing the Palo Alto plates

stops.name: Posillipo, Villa Maria above the bay
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia states plainly that the two bought Villa Maria at Posillipo in 1880, so the c.1870 hedge carried by other accounts is dropped; no month, January defaulted. The villa's exact street address is not located and the coordinate is an approximate Posillipo coastal position. it.wikipedia identifies the companion as Madame Vilbort, wife of Joseph Vilbort, director of the Paris paper Le Globe. The claim that Francesca Gallone, born at Naples in 1871, was his daughter rests on Marta Braun's research as relayed by later scholars, a book I did not read, and is [R].
stops.campa: He buys a villa on the Posillipo shore with Marie-Antoinette-Elvire Vilbort, wife of Joseph Vilbort, who edits the Paris paper Le Globe. Her health wants the climate. From here his year has two halves: the Paris winter of academies and committees, and the Naples months of fish, waves, and light strong enough to photograph in. A girl born at Naples in 1871, Francesca Gallone, is introduced by him as a niece. Modern biographers make her his daughter, and the record he left says nothing either way.
sources: Marta Braun, Picturing Time (University of Chicago Press, 1992), at second hand
suggested_refs: Villa Maria, Posillipo, Naples

stops.name: 11 boulevard Delessert, the soirée for Muybridge
stops.date_confidence: attested. fr.wikipedia confirms 11 boulevard Delessert as his address from 1881 to 1904 and gives 48.85896, 2.28664, used here. Coordinate discrepancy flagged and not resolved: muybridge.journey.json carries 48.858, 2.288 for the same apartment, the pool's afterlife lens a third value at 48.858, 2.2817, and the interlock lens reported a fourth, 48.8566, 2.2833, matching none of them. The sourced fr.wikipedia figure is preferred over byte-identical inheritance of an unsourced one; the operator can overrule.
stops.campa: He has taken an apartment in Passy, below the Trocadéro, and on the evening of the twenty-sixth of September he fills it with the science of Paris to meet Eadweard Muybridge, who turns his zoopraxiscope in front of Helmholtz and the men of the laboratories. The two have been writing for three years. Seen close, the bird pictures do not have the precision Marey needs: twelve cameras give twelve viewpoints of twelve different instants, and he wants one lens looking at one thing. The evening settles only that the instrument will have to be photographic. He builds it himself, in Naples, the following February.
sources: muybridge.journey.json, stop: Paris, Marey's soirée and the meeting of the motion-hunters
suggested_refs: 11 boulevard Delessert, Paris 16e, and its commemorative plaque
Meissonier's companion soirée for Muybridge, boulevard Malesherbes, days later

stops.name: Naples, the photographic gun finished
stops.date_confidence: the 1882 gun and its twelve-frames-a-second mechanism are attested by en.wikipedia and hekint.org; the completion at Naples with the Paris shutter-maker Otto Lund comes from the dossier's narrative alone, so the Naples siting is [R] and the villa coordinate stands in for a workshop that is not located. February is the dossier's month. The Janssen precedent is [A]: Marey names Janssen himself in Movement, chapter VII.
stops.campa: The thing he described to Tissandier gets built at Naples with the help of a Paris shutter-maker, Otto Lund. It has the shape of a rifle, a barrel holding the lens and a clockwork breech. The clockwork turns twelve times a second; a slotted disc opens for about one seven-hundred-and-twentieth of a second at each turn; behind it a glass plate steps round and takes twelve small images in a single sweep. You aim it at a gull and pull the trigger. Jules Janssen had built such a mechanism to shoot the transit of Venus.
stops.quote: It remained for Mr. Muybridge, of San Francisco, to discover, by means of a rather different method to that of Janssen, the analysis of equine locomotion, as well as that of man and various animals.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Movement, tr. Eric Pritchard (D. Appleton and Company, New York, 1895), ch. VII
suggested_refs: The fusil photographique, Musée Marey, Beaune
Jules Janssen's revolver photographique, built for the 1874 transit of Venus

stops.name: Institut de France, the gun described to the Académie des sciences
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier gave 27 March 1882; fr.wikipedia's articles on the fusil photographique and on chronophotographie independently both give 13 March 1882 for the first communication of results, and that date is taken. The 10 April 1882 presentation of gull and bat sequences is confirmed and is carried in the same stop. The primary Comptes rendus were not consulted for either date.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of March he tells the Académie des sciences what the gun has done. On the tenth of April he brings the results in: gulls in the air, and bats, each bird broken into twelve postures on one plate, a whole wingbeat laid out along the plate to be read the way a sentence is read. Nobody in the room has ever seen a bird do this. Neither, in the ordinary sense, has Marey. He has seen a photographic plate, and the seeing happens afterwards, by anybody, at leisure.
suggested_refs: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, 13 March and 10 April 1882

stops.name: Boulogne, ground for a laboratory with no roof
stops.date_confidence: coordinate corrected, and this is the most consequential correction in the pool. The Station and the later Institut Marey stood on the land now occupied by Roland-Garros, not at the Parc des Princes football stadium: fr.wikipedia's Institut Marey article gives 48.8467, 2.2506, and its Stade Roland-Garros article confirms Court No. 1 was built on the former Institut Marey site. The geography lens's wrong value was repeated at five indices and is corrected at all of them. fr.wikipedia dates the creation to 1882 against the lens's 1881; May is a default month. The military funding rationale is the dossier's.
stops.campa: The City of Paris and the Ministry of War between them give him some three thousand five hundred square metres at the edge of the Bois de Boulogne. France has lost a war eleven years earlier and wants to know how far a soldier can march under how much weight. Marey wants to know how anything moves at all. He lays a long circular track, raises a wall of black cloth behind it, rules the ground with calibrated marks, and mounts a camera in a hut that runs on rails. There is no roof and there are no walls. The whole installation is built around the sun and works only in daylight, and only in fine weather.
stops.quote: The Physiological Station, endowed by the State and the City of Paris, has afforded in this respect unique opportunities, and there, with new appliances, the following investigations have been for the most part carried out.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Movement, tr. Eric Pritchard (D. Appleton and Company, New York, 1895), Preface
suggested_refs: The Station physiologique, Parc des Princes, Boulogne, on the ground now within Roland-Garros

stops.name: Institut de France, one plate and many moments
stops.date_confidence: the 3 July 1882 presentation is fr.wikipedia's chronology; hekint.org confirms the 1882 origin of chronophotography without an exact day, and the primary Comptes rendus record was not consulted.
stops.campa: In July he presents the method that supersedes the gun. One lens, fixed. One glass plate, fixed. In front of them a disc with slots cut in it, spinning, so that each slot opens the lens for an instant as the subject crosses a black background. What comes back is a single photograph carrying ten or twenty moments of the same body at once, overlaid along the path the body took. Time becomes a distance across one picture, and a distance can be measured with a ruler.
stops.quote: If we knew under what conditions the maximum of speed, force, or labour which the living being can furnish, may be obtained, it would put an end to much discussion, and a great deal of conjecture, which is to be regretted.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), Introduction, pp.2-3
suggested_refs: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, 3 July 1882

stops.name: Station physiologique, the man reduced to points and rods
stops.date_confidence: 1883 and the method are attested in en.wikipedia; no month, January defaulted. The pin is the corrected Station physiologique site.
stops.campa: Overlaid images smear into each other when the body is broad, so Marey and his assistant Georges Demenÿ dress the runner in black velvet from crown to boot and fix bright metal buttons at every joint and bright rods along the limbs. Against the black wall the man disappears. What the plate records is a constellation of dots stepping along a line, joined by strokes, a body with nothing left of it but its geometry in time. He had proposed something of the kind in print ten years earlier, working from figures drawn by hand.
stops.quote: But it has occurred to us that, by depicting on the apparatus figures constructed with care, and representing faithfully the successive attitudes of the body during walking, running, &c., we might reproduce the appearance of the different kinds of progression employed by man.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), on the synthetic reproduction of the paces
suggested_refs: The black marker suit of the Station physiologique, 1883

stops.name: Paris, president of the aeronauts
stops.date_confidence: 1884 is attested for the presidency of the Société française de navigation aérienne; the pool tags it [A] on academie-medecine.fr in one lens and [R] in another for the same fact, and the inconsistency is flagged rather than resolved. No month, March defaulted. The society's rooms are not pinned and the corpus's general Paris coordinate stands in.
stops.campa: The society of aerial navigation elects him president. Its members have spent twenty years building machines with flapping wings, on the reasoning that birds fly by flapping and birds fly. Marey's photographs of gulls are the best evidence anybody holds about what a wing actually does, and what they show is that the beat is closer to a screw than to a row, and that the bird is held up mostly by going forward. He and Victor Tatin turn the society toward the fixed wing.
stops.quote: Whether man has endeavoured to utilize to the utmost his own motive power, and that of the animals; whether he has sought to extend his domain, to open a way for himself in the seas, or to rise into the air, it is always from nature that he has drawn his inspirations.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Animal Mechanism (D. Appleton and Company, New York), Introduction, pp.1-2

stops.name: Académie de médecine, contaminated water and the cholera

stops.campa: Cholera reaches Beaune, the town he was born in, and on the fourteenth of October Marey comes to the academy with a memoir called Les Eaux contaminées et le choléra. The argument is made the only way he ever makes one, which is from distribution: where the cases fall, where the water comes from, what the two patterns have in common and where they part. The instrument this time is a map and a table, not a drum and a stylus. He does not turn the graphic method on a population again.

stops.name: Institut de France, from a strip of paper to celluloid
stops.date_confidence: the 29 October 1888 presentation is the dossier's and was not re-checked against the Comptes rendus, so it is [R]; the 1888 paper-strip work in general and the 1889 celluloid chronophotographe are both [A] in en.wikipedia. stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of October he shows the academy a camera that runs a strip of sensitised paper past the lens, about twenty images a second. The paper tears and it stretches, and a stretched image cannot be measured. Within the year he has transparent celluloid of the kind George Eastman is selling and a camera in which a pressure plate slams the strip still for the instant of exposure and a spring jerks it on between frames. There are no sprocket holes in the strip and no projector to run it through. The strip comes out of the camera and goes onto a bench, under a rule.

Dickson then punches with holes. How much of that turn belongs to this afternoon is argued about still.

stops.campa: Le Vol des oiseaux gathers fifteen years of the question that has held him longest. Plates, diagrams, the figure of eight a wingtip cuts through the air, models built in brass to test whether a shape that flies can be made and not only described. The rule he works by he had set down in the introduction to an earlier book and never departed from: imitate nature, because nature has solved the problem already. Masson prints the book in Paris in 1890, and Marey is sixty years old.
stops.quote: We shall then attempt to analyse the rapid acts which are produced in the flight of insects and of birds; afterwards we shall endeavour to imitate nature, and we shall see, once more, that by seeking inspiration from her we have the best chance of solving the problems which she has solved.

stops.campa: At the villa he turns the camera on fencers, two men in white lunging and recovering above the water. The strips survive. What they hold is not a sport but a set of measurements: the arm's extension set against the front foot's landing, frame after frame, with the bay behind them out of focus and irrelevant. He and his staff make hundreds of such strips over these years, of men walking, running, climbing, carrying weights up and down a slope. The body in front of the lens is always doing work of some kind, and the apparatus does not change from one strip to the next.

Nothing in the frame has a joint that could be marked with a button, and nothing there could be dressed in black velvet. A wave rises, breaks, and flattens out, and the film holds the shape of a motion that belongs to no body. The method built to follow a horse's leg follows the sea. stops.campa: In the station's tanks he films eels, rays, and fish, after the same thing he was after in the horse and the gull: which part of the body does the work, and in what order the parts take their turn. An eel has no limbs to mark. The wave that runs the length of it is the whole of its locomotion, and on film that wave can be measured exactly as the wave in the bay outside was measured. He first wrote to this station for a living torpedo fifteen years ago, and he still spends half of every year here.

Demenÿ wants the apparatus, built with public money, to throw images on a screen for a paying audience; there is a machine of his own, the Biographe, and there are patents in it. Marey holds that the Station exists to measure and for nothing else whatever. Demenÿ loses his post that year and patents the Biographe in July. stops.name: Station physiologique, the cat that falls
stops.date_confidence: the falling-cat sequence is attested to this period by en.wikipedia without a precise date; June 1894 is a placement for ordering. The surviving negative is held by the Science Museum Group as part of object 1952-75, a 36-frame sequence, confirmed directly from the museum's online record.
stops.campa: A cat is held upside down by the paws and let go. Sixty frames a second catch what happens between the hands and the floor: the animal folds at the middle, twists its front half one way and its hind half the other, unfolds, and arrives on its feet, having turned itself over without pushing against anything at all. Physicists look at the plate and say that it cannot be done. The plate does not withdraw. The sequence runs to thirty-six frames, and the negative survives.

Eric Pritchard translates it into English the following year and says in his own note that the works of Muybridge can be read by anybody who reads English while the works of Marey are shut to almost everyone, which is why he has troubled to do it. The Société française de photographie makes Marey its honorary president the same year. He is sixty-four.
stops.quote: The graphic method, with its various developments, has been of immense service to almost every branch of science, and consequently many improvements have of late been effected.
stops.quote_source: Étienne-Jules Marey, Movement, tr. Eric Pritchard (D. Appleton and Company, New York, 1895), Preface, opening sentence

Marey's own stated position, crediting the Lumières rather than himself with cinema, reaches me only as the dossier's characterisation with no quotation behind it, and is [R].

In December of the same year, in a basement on the boulevard des Capucines, the Lumière brothers show paying customers a moving picture thrown on a screen, using film punched with holes along its edges so that it can be pulled exactly and identically past the gate every time. Marey's film has no holes, because measuring does not require them. Asked afterwards who invented the cinema, he says the Lumières did.
stops.quote: Every one knows the ingenious optical instrument invented by Plateau, and called by him 'Phenakistoscope.' This instrument, which is also known by the name of Zootrope, presents to the eye a series of successive images of persons or animals represented in various attitudes.

Every laboratory in Europe builds its own recording instruments, and no two of them write the same curve for the same event, so no result obtained in one can be checked against a result obtained in another. A physiology whose findings cannot be compared is not yet a science. He proposes an international institute whose entire business would be making the instruments agree.

What began as one man's irritation at tracings that could not be set beside each other becomes an international undertaking, and it will carry his name. He is sixty-eight. The founding of it, the money, the ground, the statutes, the arguing with ministries, will take up most of the six years he has left. Samuel Pierpont Langley of the Smithsonian, who has been flying steam-driven models over the Potomac and cannot see the air his wings are working in, offers to pay for research into precisely that. Langley wants a machine that will fly; Marey wants a photograph of what a wing does to the air it passes through. The offer is recorded; nothing that came of it is.

stops.name: Station physiologique, fifty-eight threads of smoke
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia's chronology gives 1901 and fifty-eight smoke trails; no month, January defaulted. The popular description of this apparatus as the first wind tunnel in the world is imprecise and is not repeated as a claim here.
stops.campa: He builds a box with a fan at one end and, at the other, a comb of fine nozzles that lay fifty-eight parallel threads of white smoke into the moving air. Air is invisible and has nothing on it that could be marked with a button, so the smoke stands in for the marks. The threads bend, part, and roll up into vortices behind the obstacle, and the camera catches them. Into the stream he puts a flat plate, then a wing, then a cylinder, and photographs each in turn.

Marey was not director for life: after his death the presidency passed to Chauveau, then Hugo Kronecker, then Charles Richet from 1911 to 1935, with Lucien Bull and Pierre Noguès running it in practice. Marey is its first director. Lucien Bull, the young Irishman working under him, has already driven the cameras up to hundreds of frames a second and patented a thirty-five millimetre chronophotographic gun in 1899. He will run the place, in practice, for decades after Marey is gone.

A lycée in Beaune already carries his name; a museum of his instruments will follow in 1955, and the vineyards still climb the slope behind the walls. The town that counts its wine by the year keeps the man who counted in twelfths of a second. In 1985 an asteroid is discovered and registered as (3456) Etiennemarey.
